1.explanation: All of the highlighting rules for Python live in src/languages/python.js inside the function exported by default(hljs). Within that function the PARAMS constant only matches parentheses, numbers, strings and hash‐comments but does not recognize ": TypeName" hints inside argument lists. Right after PARAMS, the anonymous object with begin:/->/ only matches the arrow token itself and stops, so the actual return type (e.g. List[float]) is never highlighted. There is also no pattern at all for PEP 484 type comments ("# type: ..."). To add full support for modern Python type annotations, we must extend PARAMS to consume colon‐type grammar, enrich the arrow‐return‐type variant to include the following type expression, and introduce a new pattern for "# type:" comments (and for generic brackets in types). This is why edits to these parts of python.js are required.
1.bug_scenario: In the screenshot we see a Python source file open in an editor. It contains several modern Python constructs that are not properly highlighted by highlight.js’s current Python grammar: type‐comment annotations (e.g. “# type: Dict[int, Any]”), PEP 484 style parameter hints (e.g. “root: TreeNode”), PEP 484 return‐type arrows (e.g. “-> List[float]”), async/await definitions with annotations (e.g. “async def coroutine(db: aio_db.DatabaseConnection) -> List[str]”) and decorator lines. None of these type‐hinted tokens receive the special styling they should, so they appear as plain text rather than as structured types.

2.explanation:
All of the type-hinting constructs appear inside the ‘function’ rule in python.js, which uses PARAMS to capture parameters and a simple /->/ rule for return types. 

• PARAMS only contains keywords, numbers, strings and comments—it knows nothing of colon-annotated parameters, identifier types and the ‘[ ]’ generic syntax. 
• The function-definition block is declared illegal on characters like ‘=’, ‘,’, and ‘;’, which prevents default values and comma-separated type annotations from being parsed inside the signature. 
• The return-type rule simply matches an arrow and treats only ‘None’ as a keyword, so arbitrary type expressions after ‘->’ aren’t highlighted. 

To fix PEP 484 highlighting, these rules must be extended to recognize colon-style annotations (including nested generic brackets), permit ‘=’ and commas in parameter lists, and tokenize bracketed type names and built-in typing constructs in both parameters and return types.
2.bug_scenario: The screenshot shows a Python file in a text editor where modern PEP 484 style type hints—parameter annotations like “db: aio_db.DatabaseConnection”, inline “# type: Dict[int, Any]” comments, and return-type arrows “-> List[str]”—are not being syntax-highlighted. Names of types, square-bracketed generics and the arrow annotations are rendered as plain text rather than receiving their own scopes.
